title: Quadratic forms
lead: A symmetric matrix defines a function of a vector, the quadratic form $q_A(\kvecx) = \kvecx\cdot(\kA\kvecx)$, of which the variance of a dataset in a direction is one. This section asks in which directions a quadratic form is largest and smallest, looks at it in new coordinates, sorts symmetric matrices by the signs their quadratic forms take, and turns that to the critical points of a function of two variables.
summary_html:
This section explored quadratic forms, functions that are defined by symmetric matrices.

  • If $\kA$ is a symmetric matrix, then the quadratic form defined by $\kA$ is the function $q_A(\kvecx) = \kvecx\cdot(\kA\kvecx)$. Quadratic forms appear when studying the variance of a dataset. If $\kC$ is the covariance matrix, then the variance in the direction defined by a unit vector $\kvecu$ is $q_C(\kvecu) = \kvecu\cdot(\kC\kvecu)=\kVu$.

    Similarly, quadratic forms appear in multivariable calculus when analyzing the behavior of a function of several variables near a critical point.

  • If $\klambdaone$ is the largest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix $\kA$ and $\klambdam$ the smallest, then the maximum value of $q_A(\kvecu)$ among unit vectors $\kvecu$, is $\klambdaone$, and this maximum value occurs in the direction of $\kvecuone$, a unit eigenvector associated to $\klambdaone$.

    Similarly, the minimum value of $q_A(\kvecu)$ is $\klambdam$, which appears in the direction of $\kvecum$, an eigenvector associated to $\klambdam$.

  • A symmetric matrix is positive definite if its eigenvalues are all positive, positive semidefinite if its eigenvalues are all nonnegative, and indefinite if it has both positive and negative eigenvalues.
  • If the Hessian $\kH$ of a multivariable function $f$ is positive definite at a critical point, then the critical point is a local minimum. Likewise, if the Hessian is negative definite, the critical point is a local maximum.

exercises.prompt:
Let's begin by looking at an example. Suppose we have three data points that form the demeaned data matrix

$$ \kA = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3 \\ \end{bmatrix}. $$
  1. Plot the demeaned data points in Figure 7.2.1. In which direction does the variance appear to be largest and in which does it appear to be smallest?
  2. Construct the covariance matrix $\kC$ and determine the variance in the direction of $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and the variance in the direction of $\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.
  3. What is the total variance of this dataset?
  4. Generally speaking, if $\kC$ is the covariance matrix of a dataset and $\kvecu$ is an eigenvector of $\kC$ having unit length and with associated eigenvalue $\klambda$, what is $\kVu$?

answer.solution:
Solution.

  1. The variance appears to be greatest in the direction of $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and smallest in the direction of $\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.
  2. In the direction of $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$, the variance is $9$, while in the direction of $\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$, the variance is $1/3$.
  3. The total variance is $9+1/3 = 28/3$.
  4. $\kVu = \kvecu\cdot(\kC\kvecu) = \klambda\kvecu\cdot\kvecu = \klambda$

exercises.prompt:
Let's look at some more examples of quadratic forms.

  1. Consider the symmetric matrix $\kD = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ \end{bmatrix}$. Write the quadratic form $q_D(\kvecx)$ defined by $\kD$ in terms of the components of $\kvecx=\left[\begin{array}{r}x_1 \\ x_2 \end{array}\right]$. What is the value of $q_D\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -4 \end{array}\right]\right)$?
  2. Given the symmetric matrix $\kA=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 5 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$, write the quadratic form $q_A(\kvecx)$ defined by $\kA$ and evaluate $q_A\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]\right)$.
  3. Suppose that $q\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}x_1 \\ x_2 \end{array}\right]\right) = 3x_1^2 - 4x_1x_2 + 4x_2^2$. Find a symmetric matrix $\kA$ such that $q$ is the quadratic form defined by $\kA$.
  4. Suppose that $q$ is a quadratic form and that $q(\kvecx) = 3$. What is $q(2\kvecx)$? $q(-\kvecx)$? $q(10\kvecx)$?
  5. Suppose that $\kA$ is a symmetric matrix and $q_A(\kvecx)$ is the quadratic form defined by $\kA$. Suppose that $\kvecx$ is an eigenvector of $\kA$ with associated eigenvalue -4 and with length 7. What is $q_A(\kvecx)$?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $q_D(\kvecx) = 3x_1^2 - x_2^2$ and $q_D\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -4 \end{array}\right]\right) = -4$
  2. $q_A(\kvecx) = 2x_1^2 + 10x_1x_2-3x_2^2$ and $q_A\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]\right) = -15$
  3. $\kA=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ \end{bmatrix}$
  4. $q(2\kvecx) = 12$, $q(-\kvecx) = 3$ and $q(10\kvecx)=300$
  5. $q_A(\kvecx) = -196$

Solution.

  1. $q_D(\kvecx) = 3x_1^2 - x_2^2$ and $q_D\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -4 \end{array}\right]\right) = -4$
  2. $q_A(\kvecx) = 2x_1^2 + 10x_1x_2-3x_2^2$ and $q_A\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]\right) = -15$
  3. $\kA=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ \end{bmatrix}$
  4. Notice that $q(2\kvecx) = (2\kvecx)\cdot(\kA(2\kvecx)) = 4\kvecx\cdot(\kA\kvecx) = 4q(\kvecx)$. In the same way, we have $q(-\kvecx) = q(\kvecx)$ and $q(10\kvecx) = 100q(\kvecx)$.
  5. $q_A(\kvecx) = \kvecx\cdot(\kA\kvecx) = -4\kvecx\cdot\kvecx = -4(49) = -196$

  1. Evaluating the following cell defines the matrix $\kD = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and displays the graph of the associated quadratic form $q_D(\kvecx)$. In addition, the points corresponding to vectors $\kvecu$ with unit length are displayed as a curve.

  3. Consider a unit vector $\kvecu=\left[\begin{array}{r}u_1 \\ u_2 \end{array}\right]$ so that $u_1^2+u_2^2 = 1$, an expression we can rewrite as $u_1^2 = 1-u_2^2$. Write the quadratic form $q_D(\kvecu)$ and replace $u_1^2$ by $1-u_2^2$. Now explain why the maximum of $q_D(\kvecu)$ is 3. In which direction does the maximum occur? Does this agree with what you observed from the graph above?
  4. Write the quadratic form $q_D(\kvecu)$ and replace $u_2^2$ by $1-u_1^2$. What is the minimum value of $q_D(\kvecu)$ and in which direction does the minimum occur?
  5. Use the previous Sage cell to change the matrix to $\kA=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and display the graph of the quadratic form $q_A(\kvecx) = \kvecx\cdot(\kA\kvecx)$. Determine the directions in which the maximum and minimum occur.

  6. Remember that $\kA=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ is symmetric so that $\kA=\kQ \kD \kQT$ where $\kD$ is the diagonal matrix above and $\kQ$ is the orthogonal matrix that rotates vectors by $45^\circ$. Notice that

    $$ q_A(\kvecu) = \kvecu\cdot(\kA\kvecu) = \kvecu\cdot(\kQ \kD \kQT\kvecu) = (\kQT\kvecu)\cdot(\kD \kQT\kvecu) = q_D(\kvecv) $$

    where $\kvecv=\kQT\kvecu$. That is, we have $q_A(\kvecu) = q_D(\kvecv)$.

    Explain why $\kvecv = \kQT\kvecu$ is also a unit vector; that is, explain why

    $$ |\kvecv|^2 = |\kQT\kvecu|^2 = (\kQT\kvecu)\cdot(\kQT\kvecu) = 1. $$
  7. Using the fact that $q_A(\kvecu) = q_D(\kvecv)$, explain how we now know the maximum value of $q_A(\kvecu)$ is 3 and determine the direction in which it occurs. Also, determine the minimum value of $q_A(\kvecu)$ and determine the direction in which it occurs.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. The maximum appears to occur in the direction of $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ and the minimum appears to occur in the direction of $\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.
  2. $q_D(\kvecx) = 3x_1^2 - x_2^2$ so that $q_D\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]\right) = 3$ and $q_D\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]\right) = -1$.
  3. The maximum value of $q_D(\kvecu)$ is $3$ in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$.
  4. The minimum value of $q_D(\kvecu)$ is $-1$ in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.
  5. The maximum appears to occur in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and the minimum in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.
  6. Use the fact that $\kQ \kQT=I$

  7. The maximum of $q_A(\kvecu)$ is $3$, which occurs when $\kvecu= \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{array}\right]$.

    The maximum of $q_A(\kvecu)$ is $-1$, which occurs when $\kvecu= \left[\begin{array}{r}-1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{array}\right]$.

Solution.

  1. The maximum appears to occur in the direction of $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ and the minimum appears to occur in the direction of $\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.
  2. $q_D(\kvecx) = 3x_1^2 - x_2^2$ so that $q_D\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]\right) = 3$ and $q_D\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]\right) = -1$.
  3. We have $q_D(\kvecu) = 3u_1^2 - u_2^2 = 3 - 4u_2^2$ so that the quadratic form only depends on $u_2$. The graph of this function of $u_2$ is a parabola that has a maximum of $3$ when $u_2=0$. Since $u_1^2 = 1-u_2^2$, this means that the maximum occurs when $u_1=\pm 1$. We therefore see that the maximum value of $q_D(\kvecu)$ is $3$ in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ as we saw from the graph.
  4. Now $q_D(\kvecu) = -1 + 4u_1^2$, which has a minimum value of $-1$ when $u_1=0$. Therefore, the minimum value of $q_D(\kvecu)$ is $-1$ in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.
  5. The graph of $q_A$ appears to be similar to the graph of $q_D$ only rotated by $45^\circ$. This means the maximum appears to occur in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and the minimum in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.

  6. Since $\kQ$ is orthogonal, we have $\kQ \kQT=I$ so that

    $$ |\kvecv|^2 = (\kQT\kvecu)\cdot(\kQT\kvecu) = \kvecu\cdot(\kQ \kQT\kvecu) = \kvecu\cdot\kvecu = |\kvecu|^2 = 1\text{.} $$

  7. Since $q_A(\kvecu) = q_D(\kvecv)$, the maximum of $q_A(\kvecu)$ is $3$, which occurs when $\kvecv = \kQT\kvecu = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$. This means that $\kvecu=\kQ\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{array}\right]$, the eigenvector of $\kA$ associated to $\klambda=3$.

    In the same way, the minimum value of $q_A(\kvecu)$ is $-1$, which occurs when $\kvecu=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{array}\right]$, the eigenvector of $\kA$ associated to $\klambda=-1$.

exercises.prompt:
This activity explores the relationship between the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix and its definiteness.

  1. Consider the diagonal matrix $\kD=\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ \end{bmatrix}$ and write its quadratic form $q_D(\kvecx)$ in terms of the components of $\kvecx=\left[\begin{array}{r}x_1 \\ x_2 \end{array}\right]$. How does this help you decide whether $\kD$ is positive definite or not?
  2. Now consider $\kD=\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}$ and write its quadratic form $q_D(\kvecx)$ in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2$. What can you say about the definiteness of $\kD$?

  3. If $\kD$ is a diagonal matrix, what condition on the diagonal entries guarantee that $\kD$ is

    1. positive definite?
    2. positive semidefinite?
    3. negative definite?
    4. negative semidefinite?
    5. indefinite?
  4. Suppose that $\kA$ is a symmetric matrix with eigenvalues 4 and 2 so that $\kA=\kQ \kD \kQT$ where $\kD=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$. If $\kvecy = \kQT\kvecx$, then we have $q_A(\kvecx) = q_D(\kvecy)$. Explain why this tells us that $\kA$ is positive definite.
  5. Suppose that $\kA$ is a symmetric matrix with eigenvalues 4 and 0. What can you say about the definiteness of $\kA$ in this case?

  6. What condition on the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix $\kA$ guarantees that $\kA$ is

    1. positive definite?
    2. positive semidefinite?
    3. negative definite?
    4. negative semidefinite?
    5. indefinite?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $q_D(\kvecx) = 4x_1^2 + 2x_2^2$ so $\kD$ is positive definite.
  2. $q_D(\kvecx) = 4x_1^2$ so $\kD$ is positive semidefinite.
    1. They are all positive.
    2. They are all nonnegative.
    3. They are all negative.
    4. They are all nonpositive.
    5. They are some positive eigenvalues and some negative ones .
  4. $\kA$ is positive definite.
  5. $\kA$ is positive semidefinite.
  6. They will be the same as before.

Solution.

  1. $q_D(\kvecx) = 4x_1^2 + 2x_2^2$. Both addends are nonnegative, and one of them is positive if $\kvecx$ is nonzero. This means that $q_D(\kvecx) \gt 0$ when $\kvecx$ is nonzero and so $\kD$ is positive definite.
  2. $q_D(\kvecx) = 4x_1^2$, which is always nonnegative. However, $q_D\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]\right) = 0$ so $\kD$ is positive semidefinite.
    1. They are all positive.
    2. They are all nonnegative.
    3. They are all negative.
    4. They are all nonpositive.
    5. They are some positive eigenvalues and some negative ones .
  4. Since we know that $q_D(\kvecy) \gt 0$ when $\kvecy$ is nonzero, we know that $q_A(\kvecx) \gt 0$ when $\kvecx$ is nonzero. Therefore, $\kA$ is positive definite.
  5. It will be positive semidefinite.
  6. They will be the same as before.

exercises.prompt:
Let's explore how our understanding of quadratic forms helps us determine the behavior of a function $f$ near a critical point.

  1. Consider the function $f(x,y) = 2x^3 - 6xy + 3y^2$. Find the partial derivatives $f_{x}$ and $f_y$ and use these expressions to determine the critical points of $f$.
  2. Evaluate the second partial derivatives $f_{xx}$, $f_{xy}$, and $f_{yy}$.
  3. Let's first consider the critical point $(1,1)$. Use the quadratic approximation as written above to find an expression approximating $f$ near the critical point.

  4. Using the vector $\kvecw = \left[\begin{array}{r}x-1 \\ y-1 \end{array}\right]$, rewrite your approximation as

    $$ f(x,y) \approx f(1,1) + q_A(\kvecw) $$

    for some matrix $\kA$. What is the matrix $\kA$ in this case?

  5. Find the eigenvalues of $\kA$. What can you conclude about the definiteness of $\kA$?

  6. Recall that $(x_0,y_0)$ is a local minimum for $f$ if $f(x,y) \gt f(x_0,y_0)$ for nearby points $(x,y)$. Explain why our understanding of the eigenvalues of $\kA$ shows that $(1,1)$ is a local minimum for $f$.

    x, y = var('x', 'y')
plot3d(2*x^3 - 6*x*y + 3*y^2, (x, 0.75,1.25), (y,0.75,1.25))

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. We have

    $$ \begin{aligned} f_x & {}={} 6x^2 - 6y = 0 \\ f_y & {}={} -6x + 6y = 0 \end{aligned} $$

    with critical points $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.

  2. We have

    $$ f_{xx} = 12x, \hspace{24pt} f_{xy} = -6, \hspace{24pt} f_{yy} = 6 $$

  3. This gives

    $$ f(x,y)\approx -1 + \frac12 12(x-1)^2 -6(x-1)(y-1) + \frac12 6(y-1)^2 $$
  4. $\kA = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -3 \\ -3 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.
  5. $\kA$ is positive definite.
  6. $f(x,y) \approx f(1,1) + q_A(\kvecw) \gt f(1,1)$ for points $(x,y)$ near to $(1,1)$.

Solution.

  1. We have

    $$ \begin{aligned} f_x & {}={} 6x^2 - 6y = 0 \\ f_y & {}={} -6x + 6y = 0 \end{aligned} $$

    which leads to the conditions $y=x^2$ and $y=x$. This gives the critical points $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.

  2. We have

    $$ f_{xx} = 12x, \hspace{24pt} f_{xy} = -6, \hspace{24pt} f_{yy} = 6 $$

  3. This gives

    $$ f(x,y)\approx -1 + \frac12 12(x-1)^2 -6(x-1)(y-1) + \frac12 6(y-1)^2 $$
  4. The matrix is $\kA = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -3 \\ -3 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.
  5. The eigenvalues are $\klambdaone=7.85$ and $\klambdatwo=1.15$, both of which are positive, which means that $\kA$ is positive definite.

  6. We have $q_A(\kvecw) \gt 0$ if $\kvecw$ is nonzero so

    $$ f(x,y) \approx f(1,1) + q_A(\kvecw) \gt f(1,1) $$

    for points $(x,y)$ near to $(1,1)$.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kA$ is a demeaned data matrix:

$$ \kA = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}. $$
  1. Find the covariance matrix $\kC$.
  2. What is the variance of the data projected onto the line defined by $\kvecu=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{array}\right]$.
  3. What is the total variance?
  4. In which direction is the variance greatest and what is the variance in this direction?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\begin{bmatrix} 3/2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $9/4$
  3. $5/2$.
  4. In the direction $\kvecu=\left[\begin{array}{r}0.79 \\ 0.62 \end{array}\right]$ where $\kVu=2.28$.

Solution.

  1. $\kC = \frac14 \kA \kA^T = \begin{bmatrix} 3/2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $\kVu = \kvecu\cdot(\kC\kvecu) = 9/4$
  3. The total variance is $\kV_x+\kV_y = 3/2+1=5/2$.
  4. The variance is greatest in the direction $\kvecu=\left[\begin{array}{r}0.79 \\ 0.62 \end{array}\right]$ where $\kVu=2.28$.

exercises.prompt:
Consider the matrix $\kA = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 4 & -3 \\ -3 & -3 & 4 \\ \end{bmatrix}$.

  1. Find $\kQ$ and $\kD$ such that $\kA=\kQ \kD \kQT$.
  2. Find the maximum and minimum values of $q(\kvecu) = \kvecx^T\kA\kvecx$ among all unit vectors $\kvecu$.
  3. Describe the direction in which the minimum value occurs. What can you say about the direction in which the maximum occurs?

answer.solution:

exercises.prompt:
Consider the matrix $\kB = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ \end{bmatrix}$.

  1. Find the matrix $\kA$ so that $q\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}x_1 \\ x_2 \end{array}\right]\right) = \left|\kB\kvecx\right|^2=q_A(\kvecx)$.
  2. Find the maximum and minimum values of $q(\kvecu)$ among all unit vectors $\kvecu$ and describe the directions in which they occur.
  3. What does the minimum value of $q(\kvecu)$ tell you about the matrix $\kB$?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kA = \kB^T\kB=\begin{bmatrix} 24 & -12 \\ -12 & 6 \\ \end{bmatrix}$.
  2. The maximum value is $30$ in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}2/\sqrt{5} \\ -1/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$ and the minimum value is $0$ in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{5} \\ 2/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$.
  3. The columns of $\kB$ are linearly dependent.

Solution.

  1. $q(\kvecx) = |\kB\kvecx|^2 = (\kB\kvecx)\cdot(\kB\kvecx) = \kvecx\cdot(\kB^T\kB\kvecx)$ so $\kA = \kB^T\kB=\begin{bmatrix} 24 & -12 \\ -12 & 6 \\ \end{bmatrix}$.
  2. The maximum value is $30$ in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}2/\sqrt{5} \\ -1/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$ and the minimum value is $0$ in the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{5} \\ 2/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$.
  3. The minimum value of $0$ says there is a vector such that $q(\kvecu) = |\kB\kvecu|^2 = 0$, which means that $\kB\kvecu=0$. So there is a nonzero vector that is a solution to the homogeneous equations, which implies that the columns of $\kB$ are linearly dependent.

exercises.prompt:
Consider the quadratic form

$$ q\left(\left[\begin{array}{r}x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{array}\right]\right) = 7x_1^2 + 4x_2^2 + 7x_3^2 - 2x_1x_2 -4x_1x_3-2x_2x_3. $$
  1. What can you say about the definiteness of the matrix $\kA$ that defines the quadratic form?
  2. Find a matrix $\kQ$ so that the change of coordinates $\kvecy = \kQT\kvecx$ transforms the quadratic form into one that has no cross terms. Write the quadratic form in terms of $\kvecy$.
  3. What are the maximum and minimum values for $q(\kvecu)$ among all unit vectors $\kvecu$?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kA$ is positive definite.
  2. $\kQ=\begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{3} & 1/\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & -1/\sqrt{3} & 2/\sqrt{6} \\ -1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{3} & 1/\sqrt{6} \\ \end{bmatrix}$ and $q_A(\kvecx) = 9y_1^2 + 6y_2^2 + 3y_3^2$
  3. The maximum value is $9$ and the minimum value is $3$.

Solution.

  1. The matrix $\kA = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 4 & -1 \\ -2 & -1 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $3$, $6$, and $9$ so $\kA$ is positive definite.

  2. $\kQ=\begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{3} & 1/\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & -1/\sqrt{3} & 2/\sqrt{6} \\ -1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{3} & 1/\sqrt{6} \\ \end{bmatrix}$. If $\kvecy=\kQT\kvecx$, then

    $$ q_A(\kvecx) = 9y_1^2 + 6y_2^2 + 3y_3^2\text{.} $$
  3. The maximum value is $9$ and the minimum value is $3$.

exercises.prompt:
Explain why the following statements are true.

  1. Given any matrix $\kB$, the matrix $\kB^T\kB$ is a symmetric, positive semidefinite matrix.
  2. If both $\kA$ and $\kB$ are symmetric, positive definite matrices, then $\kA+\kB$ is a symmetric, positive definite matrix.
  3. If $\kA$ is a symmetric, invertible, positive definite matrix, then $\kA^{-1}$ is also.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $q(\kvecu) = |\kB\kvecu|^2 = \klambda \geq 0$.
  2. $q_{A+B}(\kvecx) = q_A(\kvecx) + q_B(\kvecx) \gt 0$.
  3. The eigenvalues of $\kA^{-1}$ are the reciprocals of the eigenvalues of $\kA$.

Solution.

  1. The matrix is symmetric because $(\kB^T\kB)^T = \kB^T(\kB^T)^T = \kB^T\kB$. If $\kvecu$ is an eigenvector having unit length, then $q(\kvecu) = \kvecu\cdot(\kB^T\kB\kvecu) = \klambda$ and $q(\kvecu) = \kvecu\cdot(\kB^T\kB\kvecu) = (\kB\kvecu)\cdot(\kB\kvecu) = |\kB\kvecu|^2 = \klambda \geq 0$.
  2. If $\kvecx$ is a nonzero vector, then $q_{A+B}(\kvecx) = \kvecx\cdot((\kA+\kB)\kvecx) = \kvecx\cdot(\kA\kvecx) + \kvecx\cdot(\kB\kvecx) = q_A(\kvecx) + q_B(\kvecx) \gt 0$.
  3. In this case, we know that the eigenvalues of $\kA$ are all positive. If $\klambda$ is an eigenvalue of $\kA$, then $1/\klambda$ is an eigenvalue of $\kA^{-1}$ so $\kA^{-1}$ is also positive definite.

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether the following statements are true or false and explain your reasoning.

  1. If $\kA$ is an indefinite matrix, we can't know whether it is positive definite or not.
  2. If the smallest eigenvalue of $\kA$ is 3, then $\kA$ is positive definite.
  3. If $\kC$ is the covariance matrix associated with a dataset, then $\kC$ is positive semidefinite.
  4. If $\kA$ is a symmetric $2\times2$ matrix and the maximum and minimum values of $q_A(\kvecu)$ occur at $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ and $\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$, then $\kA$ is diagonal.
  5. If $\kA$ is negative definite and $\kQ$ is an orthogonal matrix with $\kB = \kQ \kA \kQT$, then $\kB$ is negative definite.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. False
  2. True
  3. True
  4. True
  5. True

Solution.

  1. False. We know that it is neither positive nor negative definite.
  2. True. This implies that $q_A(\kvecu) \geq 3$ for all unit vectors $\kvecu$. Then for any other vector $q_A(\kvecx) =q_A(|\kvecx|\kvecu)= |\kvecx|^2 q_A(\kvecu) \gt 0$.

  3. True. If $\klambda$ is an eigenvalue with associated unit eigenvector $\kvecu$, then

    $$ q_C(\kvecu) = \kvecu\cdot(\kC\kvecu) = \frac1N\kvecu\cdot(\kA \kA^T\kvecu) = \frac1N(\kA^T\kvecu)\cdot(\kA^T\kvecu) = \frac1N|\kA^T\kvecu|^2 \geq 0\text{.} $$
  4. True. The matrix $\kQ=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}$ is the identity so $\kA = \kQ \kD \kQT = \kD$.
  5. True. In this case, $\kA$ and $\kB$ are similar so they have the same eigenvalues, all of which are negative.

exercises.prompt:
Determine the critical points for each of the following functions. At each critical point, determine the Hessian $\kH$, describe the definiteness of $\kH$, and determine whether the critical point is a local maximum or minimum.

  1. $f(x,y) = xy + \frac2x + \frac2y$.
  2. $f(x,y) = x^4 + y^4 - 4xy$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $(\sqrt[3]{2}, \sqrt[3]{2})$ is neither a local maximum nor minimum.
  2. $(0,0)$ is neither a local maximum nor minimum. Both $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$ are local minima.

Solution.

  1. $$ \begin{aligned} f_x & {}={} y - \frac2{x^2} = 0 \\ f_y & {}={} x - \frac2{y^2} = 0 \end{aligned} $$

    so $x^2y=2$ and $xy^2=2$. Therefore, $xy(x-y)=0$ so $x=y=\sqrt[3]{2}$.

    Also, $f_{xx} = \frac4{x^3}$, $f_{xy} = 1$, and $f_{yy} = \frac4{y^3}$ so that the Hessian matrix is $\begin{bmatrix} 1/2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1/2 \end{bmatrix}$. The eigenvalues are $-1/2$ and $3/2$ so this matrix is indefinite and the critical point is neither a local maximum nor minimum.

  2. $$ \begin{aligned} f_x & {}={} 4x^3 - 4y = 0 \\ f_y & {}={} 4y^3 - 4x = 0 \end{aligned} $$

    so $x=y^3$ and $y=x^3$. Therefore, $x=x^9$ so $x=y=0$, $1$, or $-1$.

    Also, $f_{xx} = 12{x^2}$, $f_{xy} = -4$, and $f_{yy} = 12{y^2}$ so that the Hessian matrix is $\begin{bmatrix} 12x^2 & -4 \\ -4 & 12y^2 \end{bmatrix}$.

    At $(0,0)$, the Hessian is indefinite so this critical point is neither a local maximum nor minimum. At both $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$, it is positive definite so the critical points are local minima.

exercises.prompt:
Consider the function $f(x,y,z) = x^4 + y^4 +z^4 - 4xyz$.

  1. Show that $f$ has a critical point at $(-1,1,-1)$ and construct the Hessian $\kH$ at that point.
  2. Find the eigenvalues of $\kH$. Is this a definite matrix of some kind?
  3. What does this imply about whether $(-1,1,-1)$ is a local maximum or minimum?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. The Hessian matrix at that point is $\kH=\begin{bmatrix} 12 & 4 & -4 \\ 4 & 12 & 4 \\ -4 & 4 & 12 \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $\kH$ is positive definite.
  3. The critical point is a local minimum.

Solution.

  1. $$ \begin{aligned} f_x & {}={} 4x^3 - 4yz = 0 \\ f_y & {}={} 4y^3 - 4xz = 0 \\ f_z & {}={} 4z^3 - 4xy = 0 \end{aligned} $$

    and all three equations are satisfied at the point $(-1,1,-1)$.

    The Hessian matrix at that point is $\kH=\begin{bmatrix} 12 & 4 & -4 \\ 4 & 12 & 4 \\ -4 & 4 & 12 \end{bmatrix}$

  2. The eigenvalues are $4$, $16$, and $16$ so $\kH$ is positive definite
  3. This implies that the critical point is a local minimum.

Figure 7.2.1 is the book’s blank coordinate grid for the reader’s own plot and is not reproduced here; the link opens Figure 7.2.8 + 7.2.9, which draws the three demeaned data points of this activity and the variance in every direction.

The solution prints the maximum’s direction here; the minimum $-1$ occurs at $\kvecu=\kQ\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{array}\right]$, the eigenvector of $\kA$ associated to $\klambda=-1$, as the answer gives.
The critical point $(\sqrt[3]{2}, \sqrt[3]{2})$ is a local minimum: its Hessian is positive definite, as the note on the solution shows.

At $x=y=\sqrt[3]{2}$ we have $x^3=y^3=2$, so $f_{xx}=\frac4{x^3}=2$ and $f_{yy}=2$: the Hessian is $\kH=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, with eigenvalues $3$ and $1$. It is positive definite, and the critical point is a local minimum.
